posts.description:
Most people bookmark hackathons.

Few actually build for them.

I’ve been going through some of the AI hackathons currently open, and there’s $250K+ in prize money across these opportunities.

More importantly, they cover different areas — AI, developer tools, agentic AI, computer vision, cloud, and AI for development.

Here are some worth checking out:

🔹 Amazon — Build, Ship, Shape
💰 $138K cash
📅 Deadline: Oct. 23
🔗 https://lnkd.in/d-FcMRS2

🔹 Nebius × NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon
💰 $50K cash
📅 Deadline: Oct. 30
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dsdEkmWw

🔹 OpenCV AI Competition 2026
💰 $20,250 cash
📅 Deadline: Oct. 26
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dSRz_gQG

🔹 Google Cloud AI Builder Cup
💰 $30K
📅 Prototype deadline: Oct. 18
✈️ Sponsored travel to Singapore for finalists
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dHSxFBZE

🔹 World Bank Group — Small AI for Development
📅 Apply by Sep. 26
✈️ Winners flown to Seoul
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dvVC5xdK

🔹 AWS CDS Agentic AI Partner Hackathon
💰 $40K in prizes
📅 Deadline: Oct. 28
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dp_y6Pbf

🔹 AMD Developer Hackathon — ACT III
📅 Oct. 12–18
🖥️ AMD GPUs + ROCm
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dxM8atn3

🔹 WeAreDevelopers × BAND — Dark Factory
💰 $6K prize pool
📅 Deadline: Oct. 5
🔗 https://lnkd.in/d8r2VZVm

🔹 IBM Bob 2.0 Hackathon
💰 $10K prize pool
📅 Sep. 25–27
⏱️ 48-hour sprint
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dcs-NCqU

And honestly, the prize money isn’t even the most interesting part.

Hackathons are opportunities to:

→ Build something outside your usual comfort zone
→ Work with new technologies
→ Meet other ambitious builders
→ Turn an idea into a working product
→ Put something substantial in your portfolio
→ Get your work in front of people you normally wouldn’t have access to

I’ve learned from my own hackathon experiences that you don’t need to have everything figured out before you start.

Pick a problem.

Build.

Test.

Iterate.

Submit.

Don’t just bookmark the hackathon.

Build for it. 🚀

Which one are you considering?

posts.description:
The winners of the Built with Opus 4.6 hackathon were a lawyer, a cardiologist, a musician, a civil engineer, and a developer.

We invited 500 builders out of 13k applications to build for a week with Claude Code, and the results were astonishing:

🥇 1st Place - CrossBeam - Michael T. Brown
A lawyer in California who built a tool to streamline housing permitting and help address statewide shortages.

🥈 2nd Place - Elisa - Jon McBee
A developer in Massachusetts who built a tool that reimagines how kids learn to code and build their own projects in the age of AI.

🥉 3rd Place - postvisit.ai - Michał Nedoszytko MD, PhD
A cardiologist in Belgium who built a tool that helps patients understand and act on their medical visits to improve treatment outcomes.

🎨 Creative Exploration of Opus 4.6 - Conductr - Asep Bagja P.
A musician in Estonia who built a tool that generates a band around you as you play — a glimpse of real-time human-AI collaboration.

🧠 “Keep Thinking” Prize - TARA – Kyeyune Kazibwe
A road engineer in Uganda who built a tool that turns dash cam footage into road investment recommendations to maximize infrastructure spending

This is the democratization of problem solving. A look at a world in which Claude can help us leave no problem unsolved

Congratulations to the winners and to all the incredible builders who participated! I’m wildly inspired by you all.

posts.description:
Three hackathons. One team. A story we have to share.

WeaveHacks 1: They showed up. They built. They lost.

WeaveHacks 2: They came back. Won Best Use of Tavily. A step forward, but they weren't done.

WeaveHacks 3: Grand prize winners. $4,000 in cash + a $5,000 Unitree Go2 Pro Quadruped Robot.

We captured the exact moment they heard their name called. Watch the video below, their reaction says everything.

Here's the part that gets us. The idea for this project came from a high schooler. They've been competing together since our very first WeaveHacks hackathon, learning from every competition, sharpening their skills, and coming back hungrier each time.

This is exactly why we built WeaveHacks. Over three events, this series has become one of the most important AI builder gatherings in the Bay Area. Not just because of the prize pools or the robot dogs, but because of what happens when you give talented people the space to keep showing up. The breakthroughs don't always happen on the first try. Sometimes it takes three.

Aetheris V.O tackled our theme of self-improving agents with a question we think the whole industry should be asking: How can AI teach you instead of just doing it for you?

Aetheris uses voice and visual overlays to guide users through complex tasks step by step, rather than autonomously taking over your screen. It sees what you see via Daily screensharing, diagnoses your intent, checks a Redis vector DB for known workflows, and when it hits something new, uses Qwen and AI at Meta's SAM model to identify UI elements in real time. Every user interaction feeds an RL loop that makes the system smarter. It learns from you to teach you better.

Human-in-the-loop. Self-improving. Exactly what we asked for.

Congratulations to Savir Dillikar, Amogh Maheshwari, Raquib Alam, Reeti Bandyopadhyay, and Spencer Liu. You've been a team since day one, and watching your arc across all three WeaveHacks has been one of the best parts of running this series.

Now... WeaveHacks 4 is on the horizon. The question on everyone's mind: can they go back to back?

Stay tuned. 👀

This past weekend, I helped build something I’m really proud of.

Our team — Dane DeGiacomo, Nate Hulbert, and myself — took 1st place at the 0–1 Hackathon at the University of Minnesota.

In just a few days, we built BidEngine — an AI platform that generates full construction proposals from project details and site photos.

But what I’m most proud of wasn’t just what we built — it was how we presented it.

We spent a lot of time thinking about the experience: making the problem obvious, creating a moment in the demo where the impact was immediately clear, and turning something technical into something anyone could understand and feel in a couple-minute pitch.

The shift from building features to telling a complete story made all the difference.

Really proud of what we pulled off as a team. Grateful for the opportunity and the experience.

posts.description:
after winning 1st for HackMIT's Voloridge prize competing solo, i've come up with a new hackathon project idea, zero coding skills required

name: lessswag (sustainability track)
impact: save ~700,000 gal of water per hackathon, the amount used for 8 billion ChatGPT queries
multi-agent system: every Human hacker takes one less cotton t-shirt than they usually do, or donates it

----

this weekend, i created ROFL, which extracts window features from time series data faster than cuDF, NVIDIA’s GPU version of pandas.

although ROFL arguably makes less of a tangible impact than other projects, i do think hackathon culture pushes us to treat everything as a maximization problem (societal impact, lines of code, etc.) and overlook simpler steps, like simply minimizing harm.

this maximalist mindset applies not only to topics like sustainability, but to projects themselves too. we reward complex architecture and higher numbers of features when it's actually better to cut unnecessary work and UI.

i came up with the idea for ROFL after noticing the redundancy of calling cuDF.rolling() multiple times in my original code. ROFL deterministically completes its fused kernels and sets tile size bounds (for autotuning later) based on features and window sizes requested by the user, and it executes modified version of Hillis Steele scans based on warp shuffles. the important part of ROFL is not many lines of code at all.

perhaps the only place where less is not more is for the number of people on a team; competing solo is fine from a technical standpoint but not as fun. this will probably be my first and last time, since i was accepted for signing up to host a hacker last week.

big thanks to the Voloridge team for taking the time to understand the implementation details, and thank you to the HackMIT organizers, judges, and everyone i talked to!

posts.description:
This past weekend, we won the SpaceXAI Challenge at ACM@CMU HackCMU.

We built an AI personal assistant, Gotchu, that makes your iMessages into an agentic task marketplace for CMU campus.

Think of the request: "move a mini fridge from Morewood Gardens to Donner for $15".
An ethics agent ensures the request adheres to our student handbook, then
our market matching agent finds an available student, settles a fair price through negotiation, and waits for both users to confirm. The transaction is then settled through our virtual currency, Railcoin.

Lastly, after sending a request we generate both a photo and video of your likeness fulfilling the task.

All through iMessage or a phone call (through the Grok Suite), with no app downloads, and a simple one-time, web-based onboarding process.

Thanks to my friends, teammates and fellow AI seniors Daphne Davila, Divya Gupta, and Thomas Kanz for building this with me over 24 hours in our old Modern Regression study room, to Fiona Whittington from the SpaceXAI team for presenting us with the award and the time to check out our project, and the HackCMU team for putting on the event.

p.s. attached an ai generated video of my likeness delivering a pizza from our local joint Pizza Pronto

🏆 Winning Team at the Claude Hackathon 🏆 & 📈 Accepted to Inside HRT 🗽

Excited to share that over the weekend, my team was one of the winning teams at the Claude Builder Hackathon at UCLA, building Agentic Automation on iOS: a voice-controlled AI agent that operates a real iPhone.

Press and hold the Action Button, speak a task, and Claude takes over, seeing your screen, picking from 20+ tools, and narrating every step through the Dynamic Island so blind and low-vision users can use any installed app (and yes, we got it to play Clash Royale...). Huge shoutout to my teammates Zachary Chung and Victoria Rojas, and thank you to the Anthropic team Claude for a great event.

Additionally, I'm thrilled to share that I was accepted into Hudson River Trading's Inside HRT program. I'll be on the Algorithm Development (Quantitative Research) track, and I'm excited to learn from the team. Huge thanks to HRT for the opportunity.

posts.description:
Huel × Lovable AI Hackathon 🚀

Thanks to Lovable for coming to Huel HQ to run a half-day hackathon for our teams.

Roughly 50 people from across the business spent a few hours building tools to solve real problems.

We had everything from centralised company brains and retail shelf image libraries to tools for ingredient sourcing, traceability and community insights.

I’m always amazed by what people can build in such a short space of time when we run these sessions!

The people closest to the problems need access to the best tools to solve them. Lovable is one of those tools, and its continued focus on security and enterprise features helps us put that capability into more people’s hands. 👏

Well done to the team from our Milton Keynes factory for taking the top prize in today’s hackathon! 🏆

🚀 The Muse Glimmer technical report is out now!
Muse Glimmer is our 30B open-weight model (Apache 2.0) that was built to run agentic workloads entirely on consumer hardware. Now you can read about the model architecture, distillation recipe, quantization, and more:

arXiv: https://lnkd.in/eSA5kFNh
Blog: https://lnkd.in/eCFV5trd
Model 🤗: https://lnkd.in/eZV479AQ

Grateful for the team I have here, this was an incredibly fun ride! Major thanks to Yoram Bachrach, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Grant Gardner, Tatiana Shavrina, PhD for the opportunity and Meta (MSL & FAIR) for continuing investing in open science and open-source AI.
